name: Gboloo Grebo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
readall_conflicts: One disagreement, reported inside the single source opened: Newman (1986: 178) says Innes (1966) describes Grebo as having two distinctive degrees of stress, but Newman himself, working with a Cape Palmas ('Seaside Grebo') speaker, was unable to identify or verify any stress phenomena. Neither Innes 1966 (only pp. 11-15 held by the project, tone/stress pages not in the archive.org excerpts) nor Innes 1967 (lending-only) could be read, so Innes's own statement and its placement rule remain unquoted. Both descriptions concern the coastal Glebo/Seaside variety, not Gboloo Grebo.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1986. Contour tones as phonemic primes in Grebo. In K. Bogers, H. van der Hulst & M. Mous (eds), The phonological representation of suprasegmentals, 175-194. Dordrecht: Foris.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Phonological analysis of Grebo (Glebo) tone; may summarise Innes on prominence.

sources.citation: Vogler, Pierre. 2024 [2017]. Contribution à la classification des langues kru (Niger-Congo). Ms., HAL hal-04390526v4, 74 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative phonology only; nothing on stress ('accent' occurs only in the idiom 'mettre l'accent sur'). §2.4, p. 7: 'Les systèmes de tons sont à trois (bassa, klao, neyo..) ou quatre registres (grebo, bété, vata..).' Grebo data cited are Glebo (Payne 1860, Innes) and Jabo; Gboloo/Gbolo/Gedebo not mentioned by name.

sources.citation: Hasselbring, Sue & Eric Johnson. 2002. A sociolinguistic survey of the Grebo language area of Liberia. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2002-074. 100 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the report (a full-text search for stress/accent full text). Section 6.2.1 Transcription difficulties, p. 48: 'Kru languages are reported to have three or four levels of tone. Grebo orthography distinguishes three tones: high, mid, and low, leaving mid unmarked.' Word lists were from Barrobo, Chedepo, Fopo, Glebo, Jabo, Sabo, Trembo, Webbo, Wedabo etc; the Gboloo-group dialects (Gedebo, Gbolo, Southern Tuobo) appear only via Ingemann & Duitsman's 1976 data reproduced pp. 13-16 and in the dialect-group tables (pp. 5, 60).

sources.citation: Innes, Gordon. 1966. An Introduction to Grebo. London: School of Oriental and African Studies. 160 pp. (Rosetta Project excerpts: contents, Ch. 1 Orthography pp. 11-13, Ch. 2 Sounds pp. 14-15 only)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.28.28) (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: The open excerpt covers consonants, vowels, nasality and root shapes (CV, CVV, CVCV) only; the tone pages of Ch. 2 (pp. 16-19) are not in the excerpt, and no statement on stress appears in the pages available. Describes Glebo/Seaside Grebo (informant J. Y. Dennis) = Southern Grebo [grj], not Gboloo.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
